title: Yara and the Visitor
premise: Property surveyor Isandro Hartwell arrives to appraise the derelict Marrow house on the edge of Hollow Creek, where the measurements refuse to stay fixed and the well on the property fills itself overnight. Waiting on the porch is Wren, the imaginary friend Isandro invented at age six and abandoned when they left town—unchanged after thirty years, and no longer willing to be dismissed. As Isandro digs through county records and their own suppressed memories, they learn the Marrow family's drowned daughter was never found, that the town once 'invited in' something at the well to make her disappear, and that the visitor has been keeping a ledger of debts ever since. To survive until sunrise, Isandro must name the town's crime aloud, return the borrowed years, and choose whether Wren is a haunting, a hostage, or the only family that ever kept a promise—ending with the well finally refilling clean and Isandro walking away with a deed, a name, and no imaginary friend left to need.
about_author: Rafael Villalobos is the pen name of a former county archivist who spent a decade cataloguing property disputes in towns that preferred their records incomplete. Their horror draws on land surveys, probate files, and the quiet violence of what a community agrees not to remember.

chapters.title: The House That Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. They arrive at the Marrow house at dusk to begin a routine appraisal, but their laser measure returns different numbers each time and the interior photographs develop with an extra doorway. The emotional beat is professional unease hardening into dread—the moment competence meets something it cannot invoice.

chapters.title: Counted Doors
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, night one. They keep the lights on and recite their ritual: nine doors, three locks, one exit. At 3 a.m. there are ten doors. The beat is the collapse of Isandro's coping mechanisms and the first hint that the house responds to being observed.

chapters.title: Someone on the Porch
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At dawn a small figure waits on the porch swing—Wren, the imaginary friend, unchanged, who greets them by a nickname only a six-year-old would know. The beat is vertiginous tenderness: comfort and horror arriving in the same body.

chapters.title: What Imaginary Means
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Isandro and Wren. Wren explains they stayed because Isandro never formally said goodbye, and that the house has been 'keeping' them. Isandro's memories of age six surface in fragments. The beat is the first crack in Isandro's insistence that they imagined it all.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The dry well behind the house is brimming by morning; the water is warm and tastes of copper. A neighbor, old Mrs. Adeyemi, warns them off and mentions the Marrow girl who 'went into the ground.' The beat is the horror widening from the house to the town.

chapters.title: County Records
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV in the Hollow Creek archive. Deeds show the Marrow parcel was never sold, only 'held in trust' since 1989, with a signature Isandro almost recognizes. The beat is investigative momentum and the first concrete evidence that something was legally, deliberately buried.

chapters.title: Nine Years Old, Again
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Isandro's childhood POV. Young Isandro and Wren play by the well; an adult in a dark coat tells them to forget what they saw at the water. The beat is dread through innocence—the reader sees what Isandro's mind has spent thirty years editing out.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren shows Isandro a ledger of names and dates in the cellar: everyone the town 'invited in,' each entry closed with the word 'paid.' Isandro's childhood nickname appears as a pending line. The beat is the shift from haunting to indictment.

chapters.title: Mrs. Adeyemi's Debt
chapters.summary: Mrs. Adeyemi's POV. She confesses that as a young woman she helped the town perform the invitation to make the Marrow girl disappear, believing it would end the drought. The beat is complicity and grief—justice outside the law begins with a witness choosing to speak.

chapters.title: Doors That Move
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The house begins rearranging itself to keep Isandro in, doors multiplying, the front porch receding like a tide. Wren holds the layout steady by standing in doorways. The beat is found family under pressure—Wren spending themselves to protect the person who forgot them.

chapters.title: The Drowned Girl's Name
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. In the parish register they find the Marrow daughter's full name, Odile, recorded as 'departed' with no death date. Saying it aloud makes the well water drop an inch. The beat is the discovery that naming is power—and a weapon the town never used.

chapters.title: Invited In
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reveals the terrible symmetry: the town invited the visitor in, and the visitor needed a keeper, so it made Wren out of a child's belief and Odile's absence. Wren is both hostage and instrument. The beat is heartbreak—the friend is also the trap.

chapters.title: Sunrise Deadline
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The ledger's pending line must be resolved by the next refill of the well, one sunrise away, or Isandro becomes an entry. They decide to stay and finish the appraisal anyway. The beat is resolve—the surveyor chooses to measure the truth instead of fleeing it.

chapters.title: The Town That Knew
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, brief vignettes. Three townsfolk—the retired sheriff, the notary, Mrs. Adeyemi—receive the same dream: the well, a name, a debt coming due. Some burn old papers; one drives toward the Marrow house with a shovel. The beat is collective guilt fracturing into flight, denial, and confession.

chapters.title: What the Water Keeps
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At the well at dusk, the water shows them the night of the invitation: Odile alive, the town chanting, the visitor taking her as payment for rain. Isandro sees their own six-year-old self watching from the tree line. The beat is traumatic reintegration—memory returning whole.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren offers to take Isandro's place in the ledger, arguing they were never real and so cannot truly be lost. Isandro refuses to accept a sacrifice from the one being the town never counted as a victim. The beat is love as refusal.

chapters.title: The Sheriff's Shovel
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The retired sheriff arrives to fill the well with concrete and bury the ledger, insisting some debts die with the men who signed them. Mrs. Adeyemi stops him at gunpoint—an old hunting rifle and an older conscience. The beat is the town's reckoning turned physical.

chapters.title: Read Aloud at Midnight
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. On the porch, Isandro reads the ledger aloud, name by name, while Mrs. Adeyemi corroborates each entry and the sheriff, broken, confirms his father's signature. The house's extra doorway opens onto the well. The beat is testimony as exorcism—justice spoken outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: The Visitor Comes Up
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, climax. The visitor rises from the refilling well to collect its pending line, wearing the shape of everyone the ledger names at once. Isandro offers it not a person but the truth: the town's confession, witnessed and recorded, the debt acknowledged. The visitor must accept acknowledgment or take the whole town. The beat is terror transfigured into reckoning.

chapters.title: Paid in Full
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The ledger closes itself; the visitor releases Wren, who begins to thin at the edges now that their purpose is done. Odile's name is finally spoken over clean water, and something in the well lets go. The beat is grief and release braided together.

chapters.title: Sunrise, Ten Doors
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At dawn the house settles to its honest dimensions, the well runs clear and cold, and Wren sits with Isandro on the porch to watch the sun come up—still there, but mortal now, fading gently as belief is no longer needed to hold them. The beat is bittersweet farewell to a friend kept too long by a promise.

chapters.title: Deed and Name
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, weeks later. Isandro files the appraisal, amends the county record with Odile Marrow's true history, and takes title to the house—not to live in, but to keep the ledger's graves tended. The final line: some families are found by what they're willing to remember. The beat is quiet, earned resolution.
